title: Does Social Media Help or Hurt Your Friendships?
metaTitle: Does Social Media Help or Hurt Your Friendships?
metaDescription: Both — it depends on how you use it. Research suggests active, personal use helps connection while passive scrolling tracks with lower wellbeing and envy.
keyFinding: Social media appears to help or hurt friendships depending on how it is used — active, personalised interaction tracks with feeling more connected, while passive scrolling tracks with lower wellbeing and more envy.
honestAnswer: Both, and the research suggests the deciding factor is how you use it rather than whether you use it. Active, personalised use — direct messages, meaningful exchanges with people you actually know — tends to be associated with feeling more connected. Passive consumption — scrolling and lurking without interacting — tends to be associated with lower wellbeing and more envy.

So it is best understood as a tool that cuts both ways. It can keep long-distance and looser friendships alive that would otherwise quietly fade, and it can also displace deeper in-person connection and feed comparison. The same platform can do either, depending largely on the behaviour.
whatDataShows: A central distinction in this research, associated with work by Moira Burke and Robert Kraut, is between active and passive use. Active use — directed, personal communication with people you know — tends to be associated with greater feelings of connection and support. Passive use — consuming others' content without interacting — tends to track with lower wellbeing. The platform is less the variable than the behaviour on it.

Social media also appears genuinely useful for maintaining friendships that distance or busyness would otherwise erode. Research on friendship maintenance and so-called weak ties suggests these tools can sustain long-distance relationships and keep looser connections warm, preserving a wider social network than people could easily maintain by other means.

On the other side, passive use is repeatedly linked to envy and downward shifts in mood, partly through the comparison mechanism: scrolling exposes you to a curated stream of other people's best moments, which tends to inflate how well you imagine others are doing. There is also a concern, supported by some research, that screen-based interaction can displace deeper in-person time rather than only adding to it.
whyItFeelsDifferent: Social media can feel like it is keeping you connected even when it is mostly keeping you informed. Passively watching a friend's updates produces a sense of being in touch, but it is not the same as the back-and-forth that actually builds closeness — and the gap between feeling connected and being connected is easy to miss from the inside.

It also feels different because the comparison is constant and one-sided. You see friends' highlights far more often and in far more detail than you once would have, which tends to make their lives look fuller and easier than yours. That steady curated input nudges perception in a predictable direction, independent of what is actually going on in anyone's life.

And the design rewards passive scrolling. The frictionless, endless feed makes lurking the path of least resistance, while the more effortful, connection-building behaviour — actually reaching out to a specific person — takes a deliberate choice. So the default behaviour tends to be the one the research associates with the worse outcomes.
whatResearchSaysToDo: The clearest implication of the active-versus-passive findings is to use the tools to interact rather than to consume. Directing your time toward messages, comments, and real exchanges with people you know is the pattern associated with feeling more connected; passive scrolling is the pattern associated with the opposite.

The maintenance research suggests social media is genuinely well suited to keeping long-distance and weaker ties alive — using it as a bridge to relationships you could not otherwise sustain, rather than as a substitute for the close ones you could see in person, plays to its actual strength.

Because passive use is the one linked to envy and lower mood, reducing aimless scrolling specifically — rather than quitting altogether — is what the pattern in the research points toward. The goal supported by the evidence is shifting the mix from consuming to interacting, not necessarily logging off entirely.
whatDoesNotHelp: Treating passive scrolling as if it were connection does not appear to help, and may quietly substitute for the active, in-person, or direct contact that actually builds closeness. Watching a friend's life unfold in a feed can feel like staying in touch while doing little of the work that friendship relies on.

Assuming the platform itself is uniformly good or bad misses the main finding. The research suggests outcomes hinge on how it is used; blaming or crediting the tool as a whole tends to obscure the active-versus-passive distinction that actually predicts the difference.

Using social media as a replacement for, rather than a supplement to, deeper connection is the pattern the displacement research flags. Where screen time crowds out in-person time with close friends, the evidence suggests that trade tends to come at a cost rather than being a neutral swap.
realNumbersInContext: This is an area where it is wise to favour the direction of the findings over precise figures, because effects vary across studies and populations and the research is still evolving. The robust, repeated pattern is the active-versus-passive split: active, personalised use is associated with greater connection, while passive consumption is associated with lower wellbeing and more envy.

Alongside that, the maintenance research consistently suggests social media is good at sustaining long-distance and weak-tie friendships that would otherwise fade — a real benefit — while passive use fuels comparison and can displace deeper contact. Rather than a single statistic, the honest summary is conditional: it helps or hurts your friendships depending mostly on whether you use it to interact or to scroll.

faqs.question: Is social media good or bad for friendships?
faqs.answer: Both, and the research suggests it depends on how you use it. Active, personalised use — direct messages and real interaction with people you know — tends to be associated with feeling more connected, while passive scrolling tends to track with lower wellbeing and more envy. The behaviour matters more than the platform.

faqs.question: What's the difference between active and passive use?
faqs.answer: Active use means directed, personal communication — messaging, commenting, and genuinely interacting with people you know. Passive use means consuming others' content without interacting, such as scrolling and lurking. Research associated with Burke and Kraut links active use with greater connection and passive use with lower wellbeing.

faqs.question: Can social media actually help me keep friends?
faqs.answer: Yes — that's one of its clearer strengths. Research on friendship maintenance and weak ties suggests these tools can sustain long-distance relationships and keep looser connections warm that distance or busyness would otherwise let fade, preserving a wider network than would be easy to maintain otherwise.

faqs.question: Why do I feel worse after scrolling?
faqs.answer: Passive use is repeatedly linked to envy and lower mood, partly through comparison: scrolling exposes you to a curated stream of other people's best moments, which tends to inflate how well you imagine others are doing. The feeling is a fairly predictable response to a filtered, one-sided input.

faqs.question: Should I quit social media to protect my friendships?
faqs.answer: The research points more toward changing how you use it than quitting outright. Shifting the mix from passive scrolling toward active interaction — and using the tools to maintain long-distance and looser ties rather than to replace in-person time with close friends — is what the evidence tends to support.
